name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
title: Security of Connected Medical Devices
answer: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware, from infusion pumps and patient monitors to imaging systems and implantable devices, against unauthorized access, data interception, and manipulation. It includes device identity, firmware integrity, network segmentation, and the clinical consequences of a compromised device. The scope extends across the device lifecycle, from design and procurement to deployment, patching, and decommissioning. It also intersects with patient safety because a security failure can alter therapy delivery or diagnostic data.

sections.body: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware, from infusion pumps and patient monitors to imaging systems and implantable devices, against unauthorized access, data interception, and manipulation. It includes device identity, firmware integrity, network segmentation, and the clinical consequences of a compromised device. The scope extends across the device lifecycle, from design and procurement to deployment, patching, and decommissioning. It also intersects with patient safety because a security failure can alter therapy delivery or diagnostic data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These devices run on embedded operating systems, often real-time or stripped-down Linux or proprietary firmware, connected through hospital networks, wireless protocols such as Bluetooth Low Energy and Wi-Fi, and sometimes cloud-based vendor platforms. Many rely on gateways or medical device servers that aggregate data and manage updates. Legacy devices may run unsupported operating systems with no patch path, while newer devices include hardware roots of trust and secure boot. The infrastructure includes network access control, firewalls, and inventory systems that track device make, model, software version, and connectivity.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Security work is done through threat modeling, software bill of materials review, vulnerability scanning that is safe for clinical devices, and coordinated disclosure with manufacturers. Teams map device communication flows, segment networks so a compromised infusion pump cannot reach electronic health records, and test patches in bench environments before clinical rollout. Penetration testing of medical devices often uses passive monitoring and protocol fuzzing rather than aggressive scanning to avoid disrupting patient care. Incident response for connected devices includes isolating a device at the network level while maintaining a manual clinical workaround.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here center on patient safety, data privacy, and manufacturer accountability. Regulations such as FDA premarket and postmarket guidance require manufacturers to provide a software bill of materials and a plan for coordinated vulnerability disclosure, while hospitals must maintain an inventory and risk management process. Provenance matters because a device's firmware, third-party libraries, and update channel determine whether a patch is authentic and whether a vulnerability is exploitable. Liability can fall on manufacturers, hospitals, or integrators when a known vulnerability leads to patient harm, and site tracking of active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies reflects the broader pressure on connected clinical systems.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous monitoring, automated vulnerability remediation, and tighter integration of device security with clinical risk management. Manufacturers are moving to secure-by-design practices, over-the-air updates with signed firmware, and machine-readable software bills of materials. Hospitals are adopting medical device security platforms that correlate device telemetry with threat intelligence and clinical workflow impact. Regulatory expectations are shifting from point-in-time premarket review to lifecycle accountability, with greater emphasis on real-world evidence of security effectiveness and faster coordinated disclosure timelines.
